title: Advanced Patterns: FILTER, QUALIFY & Chaining
objective: After this lesson you will be able to restrict window inputs with FILTER, emulate QUALIFY in SQLite/PostgreSQL, chain windows through CTE stages, and combine windowed subqueries with set operations for multi-cut analyses.
why: Real analyses layer windows: rank, then aggregate the ranks; filter inputs per-function; express 'top quartile per role' without nesting three deep. These composition patterns turn single-window queries into window *programs* — and the QUALIFY gap (beloved in Snowflake/BigQuery, absent in SQLite/PG) is the portability trap every cross-engine analyst must master.

blocks.text: **`FILTER (WHERE …)`** restricts one aggregate's input rows without touching others: `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE completed = 1)` counts completions while sibling aggregates see everything. Unlike CASE-inside-aggregate (equivalent, noisier), FILTER states intent per function — and unlike query-level WHERE, it doesn't starve other columns. Supported in SQLite and PostgreSQL for aggregates (not for ranking/navigation functions).

blocks.code:
-- Per-course totals + completions side by side, one grouped pass (real SQLite/PostgreSQL)
SELECT course_id,
  COUNT(*) AS total,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE completed = 1) AS done,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE completed = 0 AND progress >= 50) AS advanced
FROM enrollments
GROUP BY course_id;
blocks.caption: FILTER: each aggregate sees its own slice of the group

blocks.text: QUALIFY doesn't exist here — emulate it

Snowflake/BigQuery offer **`QUALIFY`** (WHERE for window aliases — filter ranks inline). SQLite and PostgreSQL don't. The emulation is the subquery wrapper from Ch.1 (compute inside, filter outside) — or a CTE stage for readability. Know the translation cold: every QUALIFY example in blog posts becomes a wrapper in your engines, mechanically.

blocks.caption: QUALIFY ≡ subquery wrapper: compute inside, filter outside

blocks.text: Chaining: windows over windows via stages

Windows can't nest directly (`RANK() OVER (… SUM() OVER …)` is illegal), but stages chain freely: CTE 1 ranks, CTE 2 aggregates the ranks ('average rank per role'), CTE 3 filters. Each stage is independently runnable — the pipeline-debugging discipline from Intermediate Ch.2, now with windowed stages. Name stages for their analytic role (ranked, summarized, shortlisted), not their mechanics.

blocks.code:
-- Chained: rank developers, then average rank per role (real SQLite/PostgreSQL)
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT role, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC) AS rnk
  FROM developers
),
by_role AS (
  SELECT role, AVG(rnk) AS avg_rank, COUNT(*) AS devs
  FROM ranked GROUP BY role
)
SELECT role, ROUND(avg_rank, 1) AS avg_rank, devs
FROM by_role ORDER BY avg_rank;
blocks.caption: Window stage feeding an aggregate stage — compose via CTEs

blocks.title: Named WINDOW + FILTER + stages compose
blocks.text: The full toolkit stacks: one WINDOW definition reused by RANK and running SUM, FILTER slicing aggregates per function, stages chaining windowed outputs into further analysis. Complexity lives in named, testable layers — never in one giant SELECT.

blocks.query: SELECT completed, COUNT(*) AS n FROM enrollments GROUP BY completed;
blocks.note: Run this slice inventory in the sandbox — the two groups FILTER will separate. Every FILTER (WHERE completed = 1) below operates on exactly these slices: verify the raw groups first, then predict each filtered count.

items: FILTER slices per-aggregate input (aggregates only, SQLite + PG); CASE-equivalent but declarative
No QUALIFY in these engines — the subquery/CTE wrapper is the mechanical translation
Windows chain through stages (CTEs), never by nesting — name stages analytically
Compose WINDOW + FILTER + stages; keep each layer independently runnable

exercise.prompt: (a) In the sandbox, run the slice inventory and record both counts. (b) In real SQLite/PostgreSQL, write a per-course dashboard row: total, done (FILTER), advanced (FILTER), pct_done — one grouped pass. (c) Wrap it: shortlist courses with pct_done < 50 via the QUALIFY-emulation wrapper, and state in one sentence why FILTER beats three separate queries.
hints: Inventory gives two numbers (completed 0/1 counts) — your FILTER aggregates must reproduce them exactly per course when summed.
Dashboard row: GROUP BY course_id with three COUNT(*) variants (plain + two FILTERs) + the 100.0 rate with NULLIF. Shortlist wraps with WHERE pct_done < 50 outside.
One sentence: single grouped pass vs three scans — FILTER shares the grouping work across metrics instead of repeating it.
exercise.solution:
-- (b) dashboard row (real SQLite / PostgreSQL)
SELECT course_id,
  COUNT(*) AS total,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE completed = 1) AS done,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE completed = 0 AND progress >= 50) AS advanced,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE completed = 1) / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 1) AS pct_done
FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;
-- (c) shortlist: SELECT * FROM (<above>) WHERE pct_done < 50;
-- FILTER wins: one grouping pass serves all metrics vs one scan per query.
exercise.why: Single-pass multi-metric queries are the production payoff of FILTER, and the wrapper rehearses QUALIFY translation once more — the two portability skills this lesson exists to teach.

quiz.q: FILTER (WHERE completed = 1) vs CASE WHEN completed = 1 THEN 1 END inside COUNT — difference?
options: Semantically equivalent for aggregates; FILTER states per-function intent more readably (and only works on aggregates)
quiz.explain: Same rows counted; different readability. FILTER's restriction (aggregates only, SQLite+PG) versus CASE's universality is the real distinction to remember.

quiz.q: Translate Snowflake's QUALIFY rnk <= 3 to SQLite/PostgreSQL.
options: Subquery/CTE wrapper: compute the window inside, filter the alias outside
quiz.explain: QUALIFY is WHERE-for-windows. Without it, the pipeline rule applies: windows evaluate after WHERE, so filtering needs an outer level. Mechanical translation, same rows.

quiz.q: Why can't windows nest (RANK() OVER (SUM() OVER …))?
options: One evaluation level per SELECT: compose through CTE stages instead, each independently runnable
quiz.explain: SQL evaluates all windows at the same pipeline stage over the same input. Multi-level analysis stages explicitly — ranked CTE feeding aggregate CTE — gaining debuggability as a bonus.

quiz.q: FILTER vs query-level WHERE for 'completions alongside totals'?
options: WHERE would starve the totals column of non-matching rows; FILTER slices per function while siblings see everything
quiz.explain: Query WHERE filters rows for all columns; FILTER filters per aggregate. Side-by-side metrics need per-function slices — FILTER (or CASE) is the only correct shape.

summary: FILTER slices per aggregate, wrappers emulate QUALIFY, stages chain windows legally, and named WINDOWs keep multi-function queries DRY. Composition patterns turn window queries into window programs.
